Interview: “This Tempting Madness” Director Jennifer E. Montgomery On Turning Real Trauma Into A Gripping Feature

Writer-director Jennifer E. Montgomery breaks down her mind-bending thriller This Tempting Madness, casting Simone Ashley, and filming real-life trauma.
By Rory Fish 2 days ago
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:13
Instaread
  • Share
  • Tweet
0

In her feature directorial debut, American filmmaker Jennifer E. Montgomery delivers a gripping, mind-bending psychological thriller with This Tempting Madness. Starring Bridgerton standout Simone Ashley alongside Austin Stowell, Suraj Sharma and Zenobia Shroff, the film follows Mia, a woman who awakens from a near-fatal fall with severe amnesia, only to discover her husband has been arrested for her attempted murder.

Blurring the lines between memory, trauma and paranoia, this complex mystery explores the terrifying reality of losing trust in one’s own perception as Mia navigates a toxic tug-of-war between her protective brother and accused husband.

Top 10 Films spoke to Montgomery, who both writes and directs the film, to discover how a deeply personal, real-life trauma inspired this haunting debut. In our exclusive interview, Montgomery reveals how she subverted classic thriller conventions to prioritise “emotional authenticity over literal authenticity,” the unique dynamic of co-writing and filming alongside her cinematographer partner Andrew Davis, and the technical craft — from vintage 12mm Panavision lenses to subverting traditional edit cuts and integrating lead actress Simone Ashley’s voice directly into the soundscape — used to drag the audience headfirst into Mia’s fractured mind.

This Tempting Madness was released in the UK on digital platforms on August 10, 2026. 

Top 10 Films: What was it about the real events behind This Tempting Madness that compelled you to turn such a personal, traumatic experience into a psychological thriller?

Jennifer E. Montgomery: The simplest answer: living the experience before any talk of a film felt like a psychological thriller. When it came down to deciding to turn lived experience into film, I really wanted to tell the story in a subversive way that would allow a wider audience to engage with the very difficult subject.

What happened was so intense we decided that the film needed to be an immersive experience for the audience, one that was solely rooted in the fractured mind of Mia, our main character, to force them not just to observe, but to actually feel her disorientation and her fear on her journey back from the brink.

T10F: When you’re fictionalising a true story with emotional weight, how do you balance authenticity with the demands of genre, tension and cinematic storytelling?

JEM: It varies depending on the true story, but in this circumstance the story was so incredible, so strange, with so many twists and turns, the real challenge was determining how to focus the narrative in a way that delivered a cathartic journey for Mia and for the audience.

Leaning into the genre and cinematic storytelling helped created the tension that comes from feeling the emotional distress of Mia, which was very real. Our rubric was to choose emotional authenticity over literal authenticity, and in so doing allowed us to deliver a journey to help make sense of the horrific experience rather than just document it.

T10F: What did your collaboration with Andrew Davis look like day to day, and how did the two of you shape Mia’s fractured perspective into something that feels both subjective and cinematic?

JEM: Andrew is both my partner in life and in creativity. Our strengths balance and offset one another. We lean into those complementary differences as we approach any project we write and develop. That extends to set, I direct and he captures the story as cinematographer, but because of the time we have spent together throughout the entire process it allows for a unique shorthand.

That isn’t to say we don’t argue, it’s more that we’ve been partners long enough we have learned how to butt heads constructively. It was a journey to shape Mia’s fractured perspective; it started from a lived experience we shared together and then extended onto the page. The script was written very subjectively and was the blueprint that guided how we collaborated with our department heads on set, and ultimately with our incredible editor.

T10F: Moving from shorts and music videos into your first feature is a huge shift; what surprised you most about the scale, pace or pressure of feature filmmaking?

JEM: It’s a huge shift! This was by no means first time working on a feature film set, so I had an idea of what I was in for, but there is so much that you just can’t know until you’ve been at the helm as the director. I quickly was reminded that the larger the ship the slower it takes to change its heading. The scale, pace and pressure delivered a keen sense of how fortunate I was to be directing my first feature, and the incredible responsibility that went along with inhabiting that chair.

T10F: What stood out about Simone Ashley during casting, and what did she bring to Mia that changed or deepened your understanding of the character?

JEM: Simone has this incredible presence and intensity that came across from moment one, it was captivating, and her commitment to the role allowed us to really push how far we could go with the subjectivity in the filmmaking. She had such a beautifully deep empathy for Mia and her suffering; but, was also very committed to finding her strength amidst the trauma. This really aligned with what we were committed to telling with this story and helped to always push towards delivering a film not about a woman falling, but about a woman rising.

T10F: With Austin Stowell, Suraj Sharma and Zenobia Shroff in the mix, how did you approach directing a cast whose characters are constantly pulling Mia — and the audience — in different emotional directions?

JEM: Every actor is different, and with that understanding it’s important to find a different and unique rhythm with each of the cast individually. That said, holistically, I encouraged the cast to put themselves aggressively in the shoes of the characters without judgement of their actions. Even when the effect was intended to mislead the audience, I didn’t want the cast to perform in a way that was inauthentic, but rather real to them in the moment.

For Austin, it was important to talk to him through the lens of what his character was experiencing in the moments leading up to the scene, to give him a sense of the inner dialogue. He did a great job of really immersing himself in the perspective of his character.

Suraj is just such a fantastic talent that I wanted to pull off the guardrails and give him space to play, which really aligned with his character who realistically spent so much time in small spaces just waiting for some measure of progress in his sister’s condition. That creates its own measure of trauma, and it became of question of what the various ways that would manifest?
Zenobia is just such a consummate professional, everyone knew when she showed up on set, it was go-time. In preparation for filming, we talked at length about her own backstory, and it was always so fun to see what subtle nuances she would bring to each scene.

I was very lucky to work such a talented cast in this film, and I’m so proud of what each of them brought to screen in their own unique way.

T10F: The film plays heavily with memory, distortion and unreliable perception; what visual or editing techniques were key to creating Mia’s fractured reality?

JEM: We used a variety of techniques to create Mia’s fractured reality; it really was a puzzle that started on the page, came to life on-set, and was pieced together in the editing room. We worked closely with Panavision to find the right lenses to help us capture the varying mental states within the film.

Visual contrast is an essential tool for any technique to be effective, and having a variety of vintage and customed tuned lenses was one of our main tools to achieve that during production.

One example, is a very particular vintage H-Series 12mm lens we used. It’s very wide but does not distort like a fisheye. This allowed us to bring Mia to the extreme foreground and combined with a precise eyeline shift to or from directly above the lens was used to show Mia transitioning in and out of states of mental dislocation.

In addition to lensing, we very carefully mapped out the complex transitions between past and present so that they would feel seamless. These transitions were built from the natural language of editing; but subverted. Traditionally you may cut from a character’s look to what they are looking at; but instead, we chose to cut from a character’s look in the present to what they are looking at in the past. This and the elliptical design of the film, were enhanced and refined in the edit.

The cadence of the edit and camera movement increased as the narrative progressed towards climax. But it wasn’t just the visual and editing techniques that were key to creating the fractured reality, so much of what delivers that is actually the sound design and the score. They were very intricately crafted to externalize what was going on inside Mia’s head, and to do that we used Simone’s voice both in the design and the score.

T10F: Looking back on the production, what’s the biggest lesson you’re taking forward as a director, and were there any moments on set that fundamentally changed how you approach storytelling?

JEM: The production was a crucible, but in the best possible way. Making a film is an act of creation, but it’s also an intense process of refinement. Although there were no moments that fundamentally changed how I approach storytelling, the experience provided the extreme heat necessary to hone my instincts. There was so much happening, so many decisions that needed to be made every second of the process, it really drove home the need for preparation but also agility. Nothing goes to plan without a plan, but it also often doesn’t even with one.
